We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t)={sin}^{3}⁡t,$ we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t)={cos}^{2}⁡t,$ we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=-1.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4},\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
